opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Paul speaks about Christ in a way that forces me to adjust how I think. Not as someone who begins in time, but as One who is before it. That’s not natural for me to grasp. It pushes against how I understand everything.
As I read Psalm 89, “My kindness is established forever,” I pause there. If that’s true, then it isn’t describing something that lasts a long time—it’s describing something that doesn’t sit inside time at all. It just is.
And then Christ is called the firstborn of the dead—not as a starting point, but as a position. Authority over death, not emergence from it.
Then I go to the Gospel of John 13. A very grounded moment—Jesus washing feet. Physical, immediate, human. But what He says doesn’t stay confined to that setting.
“No servant is greater than his master… whoever receives the one I send receives me… and whoever receives me receives the One who sent me.”
That’s not just instruction. That’s identity and continuity.
And then He says:
“I tell you this now, before it happens… so that you may believe that I AM.”
That line doesn’t read like a prediction. It reads like awareness—complete awareness.
He speaks of betrayal—“the one who ate my food has raised his heel against me”—drawing from Psalm 41. What stands out to me is not just that it will happen, but that it is already fully known to Him.
This is where I start reaching a bit.
Because in physics, there’s this idea—very simplified—that time might not just be a straight line we move along, but something more like a structure. Something that, in theory, could be seen all at once rather than experienced step by step. I know that analogy has limits. But it helps me approach this:
That which is unfolding for us… is not unfolding for Him in the same way.
So when Scripture speaks of things to come as if they are already established, it’s not confusion. It’s perspective. God is not moving through time as we are. He is present to all of it.
And then something shifts for me.
Because that means the crucifixion was not a disruption. The betrayal was not unforeseen. None of it was outside His knowing. And yet—He steps into it anyway.

That’s the part that lands differently. Because if Christ stands both within time and beyond it, then what He does is not create eternity or “allow” it in a casual sense. Eternity already is. But He opens what was closed. He reconnects what was separated. So when I hear, “My kindness is established forever,” I don’t hear duration anymore. I hear stability. Something unchanging, something already complete. And I’m still trying to understand it. I don’t think I fully will. But I can see this much:

Christ is not confined to the sequence I live in.
He sees the whole of it.
And somehow, within that full knowledge—
He still chooses to enter it, to act, and to draw us back into something that does not end.
That’s where the precision ends for me…
and something deeper begins.
